summary: Defines the Basic HTTP authentication scheme, which transmits credentials as a user-id and password pair encoded with Base64. The encoding is not encryption, so it should only be used over a secure connection.

plainLanguage.summary: Basic authentication is the simplest way to ask for a username and password on the web: the server sends a challenge, the browser sends the credentials back in a header, and the two are joined with a colon and encoded so that they contain only safe characters. The encoding is not encryption, so the header still has to travel over an encrypted connection.

questions: how does basic auth encode credentials
what is the charset parameter in basic auth
subtitle: How a browser sends a username and password in an HTTP header, and why that is only safe inside an encrypted connection.

tldr.problem: HTTP needed a simple way for a server to ask for a username and password and for the client to send them back. The earlier definition, RFC 2617, did not say how the two characters should be encoded, which broke when a password contained anything outside plain ASCII.
tldr.mechanism: The client joins the user identifier, a colon and the password, encodes the result as octets and then encodes those octets in Base64. A new charset authentication parameter tells the client which encoding the server expects, and the only allowed value is UTF-8.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7617 is a Proposed Standard from September 2015 that updates the definition of the Basic scheme in RFC 2617. The RFC states plainly that the scheme is not a secure method of authentication unless it is used with an external secure system such as TLS, because the credentials travel as cleartext.

facts.label: Credentials encoding
facts.value: Base64 of the user-id, a colon and the password

today: RFC 7617 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2015. It obsoletes RFC 2617 for the Basic scheme, together with RFC 7235, RFC 7615 and RFC 7616, and no later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This document defines the Basic HTTP authentication scheme, which transmits credentials as user-id and password pairs encoded using Base64. HTTP authentication schemes are defined in RFC 7235.

The scheme is not considered to be a secure method of user authentication unless it is used in conjunction with some external secure system such as TLS, as the user-id and password are passed over the network as cleartext.

The Basic scheme was previously defined in Section 2 of RFC 2617. This document updates the definition and also addresses internationalization issues by introducing the charset authentication parameter. Other documents updating RFC 2617 are HTTP/1.1 Authentication, RFC 7235, which defines the authentication framework; HTTP Digest Access Authentication, RFC 7616, which updates the definition of the Digest scheme; and HTTP Authentication-Info and Proxy-Authentication-Info Response Header Fields, RFC 7615. Taken together, these four documents obsolete RFC 2617. The terms protection space and realm are defined in Section 2.2 of RFC 7235, and the terms character repertoire and character encoding scheme in Section 2 of RFC 6365.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC takes over the Basic scheme from an older document, tidies its wording to match the current HTTP authentication framework, and adds a way to say that the server wants passwords encoded as UTF-8.

sections.title: The Basic Authentication Scheme
sections.content:
The scheme is based on the model that the client needs to authenticate itself with a user-id and a password for each protection space, or realm. The realm value is a free-form string that can only be compared for equality with other realms on that server, and the server services the request only if it can validate the user-id and password for the protection space applying to the requested resource.

In challenges, the scheme name is Basic, the authentication parameter realm is REQUIRED, and the authentication parameter charset is OPTIONAL. No other authentication parameters are defined: unknown parameters MUST be ignored by recipients, and new parameters can only be defined by revising the specification. Both scheme and parameter names are matched case-insensitively.

For credentials, the token68 syntax of RFC 7235 is used. Upon receipt of a request for a URI within the protection space that lacks credentials, the server can reply with a challenge using the 401 Unauthorized status code and the WWW-Authenticate header field, for example HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized with WWW-Authenticate: Basic realm="WallyWorld", where WallyWorld is the string assigned by the server to identify the protection space. A proxy can respond with a similar challenge using the 407 Proxy Authentication Required status code and the Proxy-Authenticate header field.

To receive authorization, the client obtains the user-id and password from the user, constructs the user-pass by concatenating the user-id, a single colon character and the password, encodes the user-pass into an octet sequence, and obtains the basic-credentials by encoding that octet sequence using Base64 into a sequence of US-ASCII characters.

The original definition failed to specify the character encoding scheme used to convert the user-pass into an octet sequence. In practice most implementations chose either a locale-specific encoding such as ISO-8859-1 or UTF-8. For backwards compatibility, this specification continues to leave the default encoding undefined, as long as it is compatible with US-ASCII, mapping any US-ASCII character to a single octet matching the US-ASCII character code.

The user-id and password MUST NOT contain any control characters. A user-id containing a colon character is invalid, because the first colon in a user-pass string separates the user-id from the password, and text after the first colon is part of the password. Many user agents produce user-pass strings without checking that user-ids supplied by users do not contain colons, in which case recipients treat part of the username input as part of the password.
sections.plainLanguage: The server names a realm and asks for credentials; the client joins the name and the password with a colon and encodes the result in Base64 so that it can travel in a header. A name that itself contains a colon cannot be sent, because the first colon is what separates the two halves.

sections.title: The charset Parameter
sections.content:
In challenges, servers can use the charset authentication parameter to indicate the character encoding scheme they expect the user agent to use when generating the user-pass octet sequence. This information is purely advisory.

The only allowed value is UTF-8, matched case-insensitively. It indicates that the server expects character data to be converted to Unicode Normalization Form C and encoded into octets using the UTF-8 character encoding scheme.

For the user-id, recipients MUST support all characters defined in the UsernameCasePreserved profile of Section 3.3 of RFC 7613, with the exception of the colon character. For the password, recipients MUST support all characters defined in the OpaqueString profile of Section 4.2 of RFC 7613. Other values are reserved for future use.

The charset is only defined on challenges, because Basic authentication uses a single token for credentials, so the credentials syntax is not extensible. The RFC notes that the name charset was chosen for consistency with Section 2.1.1 of RFC 2831, and that a better name would have been accept-charset, as it is not about the message it appears in but the server's expectation.

In the example, the server prompts for authentication in the foo realm using Basic authentication with a preference for UTF-8: WWW-Authenticate: Basic realm="foo", charset="UTF-8". The parameter value can be either a token or a quoted string; in this case the server chose the quoted-string notation. The user's name is test, and the password is the string 123 followed by the Unicode character U+00A3, the pound sign. Using UTF-8 the user-pass becomes the characters 't' 'e' 's' 't' ':' '1' '2' '3' and the pound sign, with octets 74 65 73 74 3A 31 32 33 C2 A3. Encoding that octet sequence in Base64 yields dGVzdDoxMjPCow==, so the Authorization header field would be Authorization: Basic dGVzdDoxMjPCow==, or, for proxy authentication, Proxy-Authorization: Basic dGVzdDoxMjPCow==.
sections.plainLanguage: The server can now say which encoding it wants, and the only option is UTF-8, with the text first put into a standard normalized form. The parameter is advice, not a demand, so a client that has never heard of it still works.

sections.title: Reusing Credentials
sections.content:
Given the absolute URI of an authenticated request, the authentication scope of that request is obtained by removing all characters after the last slash character of the path component. A client SHOULD assume that resources identified by URIs with a prefix match of the authentication scope are also within the protection space specified by the realm value of that authenticated request.

A client MAY preemptively send the corresponding Authorization header field with requests for resources in that space without receipt of another challenge from the server. Similarly, when a client sends a request to a proxy, it MAY reuse a user-id and password in the Proxy-Authorization header field without receiving another challenge from the proxy server.

For example, given an authenticated request to http://example.com/docs/index.html, requests to http://example.com/docs/, http://example.com/docs/test.doc and http://example.com/docs/?page=1 could use the known credentials, while http://example.com/other/ and https://example.com/docs/ would be considered outside the authentication scope. A URI can be part of multiple authentication scopes, such as http://example.com/ and http://example.com/docs/, and this specification does not define which of these should be treated with higher priority.
sections.plainLanguage: Once a client has authenticated for one address, it can reuse the same credentials for everything below the last slash of that path, without waiting to be challenged again. A URI that differs in another way, such as the same path over https, lies outside that scope.

sections.title: Internationalization Considerations
sections.content:
User-ids or passwords containing characters outside the US-ASCII character repertoire will cause interoperability issues, unless both communication partners agree on what character encoding scheme is to be used. Servers can use the charset parameter to indicate a preference of UTF-8, increasing the probability that clients will switch to that encoding.

The realm parameter carries data that can be considered textual, but RFC 7235 does not define a way to reliably transport non-US-ASCII characters. The RFC notes that this is a known issue that would need to be addressed in a revision to that specification.
sections.plainLanguage: Anything outside plain ASCII needs both ends to agree on an encoding, which is what the charset parameter is for. The realm name itself still has this problem, and the RFC leaves it to a later revision of the HTTP authentication document.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The Basic authentication scheme is not a secure method of user authentication, nor does it in any way protect the entity, which is transmitted in cleartext across the physical network used as the carrier. HTTP does not prevent the addition of enhancements such as schemes to use one-time passwords.

The most serious flaw of Basic authentication is that it results in the cleartext transmission of the user's password over the physical network, and many other authentication schemes address this problem. Because Basic authentication involves the cleartext transmission of passwords, it SHOULD NOT be used, without enhancements such as HTTPS, to protect sensitive or valuable information.

A common use of Basic authentication is for identification purposes, requiring the user to provide a user-id and password as a means of identification, for example to gather accurate usage statistics on a server. When used in this way it is tempting to think that there is no danger in its use if illicit access to the protected documents is not a major concern. This is only correct if the server issues both the user-id and the password to the users and, in particular, does not allow the user to choose their own password. The danger arises because naive users frequently reuse a single password to avoid the task of maintaining multiple passwords.

If a server permits users to select their own passwords, the threat is not only unauthorized access to documents on the server but also unauthorized access to any other resources on other systems that the user protects with the same password. Furthermore, in the server's password database, many of the passwords may also be users' passwords for other sites, so the owner or administrator of such a system could expose all users of the system to the risk of unauthorized access to all those other sites if this information is not maintained in a secure fashion. This raises both security and privacy concerns. If the same user-id and password combination is in use to access other accounts, such as an email or health portal account, personal information could be exposed.

Basic authentication is also vulnerable to spoofing by counterfeit servers. If a user can be led to believe that she is connecting to a host containing information protected by Basic authentication when, in fact, she is connecting to a hostile server or gateway, then the attacker can request a password, store it for later use, and feign an error. Server implementers ought to guard against this kind of counterfeiting; in particular, software components that can take over control of the message framing on an existing connection need to be used carefully or not at all.

Servers and proxies implementing Basic authentication need to store user passwords in some form in order to authenticate a request. These passwords ought to be stored in such a way that a leak of the password data does not make them trivially recoverable. This is especially important when users are allowed to set their own passwords, since users are known to choose weak passwords and to reuse them across authentication realms. Servers ought to avoid storing user passwords in plaintext or as unsalted digests. The use of the UTF-8 character encoding scheme and of normalization introduces additional security considerations.
sections.plainLanguage: Base64 is an encoding, not a cipher, so anyone who can read the traffic can read the password. The RFC therefore says the scheme should not be used to protect anything sensitive unless the connection is encrypted, and warns about servers that keep the passwords in a form that is easy to reverse.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 2617
sections.content:
The scheme definition has been rewritten to be consistent with newer specifications such as RFC 7235.

The new authentication parameter charset has been added. It is purely advisory, so existing implementations do not need to change, unless they want to take advantage of the additional information that was previously not available.

The document takes over the definition of the Basic scheme from RFC 2617, and the acknowledgements of that document still apply, with significant amounts of text borrowed from it.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules themselves did not change. The only addition is the charset parameter, which old clients can safely ignore.

sections.title: Deploying the charset Parameter
sections.content:
For user agents, those not implementing charset will continue to work as before, ignoring the new parameter, and those that already default to the UTF-8 encoding implement it by definition. Other user agents can keep their default behaviour and switch to UTF-8 when they see the new parameter.

For servers, those that do not support non-US-ASCII characters in credentials do not require any changes, and those that need to support them but cannot use UTF-8 are unaffected, continuing to function as well or as badly as before. Servers that need to support non-US-ASCII characters and can use UTF-8 can opt in by specifying the charset parameter in the authentication challenge. Clients that understand it will then start to use UTF-8, while other clients will continue to send credentials in their default encoding, broken credentials, or no credentials at all. Until all clients are upgraded to support UTF-8, servers are likely to see both UTF-8 and legacy encodings in requests. When processing as UTF-8 fails, because of a failure to decode as UTF-8 or a mismatch of user-id and password, a server might try a fallback to the previously supported legacy encoding to accommodate those clients. Such implicit retries need to be done carefully, since some subsystems detect repeated login failures and treat them as a potential credentials-guessing attack.

The RFC explains why the default encoding was not simply switched to UTF-8. There are sites in use today that default to a local character encoding scheme such as ISO-8859-1 and expect user agents to use that encoding, and authentication on those sites will stop working if the user agent switches to UTF-8. Sites might even inspect the User-Agent header field to decide which character encoding scheme to expect from the client, so they might support UTF-8 for some user agents and default to something else for others, and those user agents will have to continue to do what they do today until the majority of these servers have been upgraded to always use UTF-8.
sections.plainLanguage: The parameter can be switched on for one server at a time. Servers that offer it will see both encodings for a while, and a client that sends the wrong encoding may be refused, so the fallback has to be done carefully.

viz.caption: THE RULES THE RFC SETS ON CREDENTIALS

items.title: realm is required
items.text: Every challenge must name the protection space with a realm value.

items.title: charset is optional
items.text: It may say UTF-8, and it is purely advisory.

items.title: One colon only
items.text: The first colon separates the user-id from the password, so a user-id may not contain one.

items.title: No control characters
items.text: The user-id and password must not contain control characters.

items.title: Base64 output
items.text: The octets are encoded in Base64 into US-ASCII characters.

items.title: Unknown parameters
items.text: Recipients must ignore authentication parameters they do not recognize.
